title: Revisiting Picard’s proof of the Picard–Weber–Weck selection theorem

paper.title: Revisiting Picard’s proof of the Picard–Weber–Weck selection theorem
paper.abstract: Abstract. Revisiting the rationale provided by Picard in the seminal paper [ 13 ] , we provide an independent, self-contained proof of the Maxwell compactness property for weak Lipschitz domains in the Euclidean setting, detouring technical complications like the differential forms setting, Gaffney’s inequality for smooth domains, Calderon’s extension theorem or regularity theory for PDEs, or systems thereof, on smooth domains that are used in this context. As a by-product we provide an independent proof of the classical Gaffney estimate for cubes using only L 2 L^{2} -completeness of the Fourier bases.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: This paper is concerned with a by-now classical compactness result for differential forms going back to several articles by Weck [ 21 ] , Weber [ 20 ] , and Picard [ 13 ] . The main contribution of all of these results is that, for the sake of the argument expressed in dimension d = 3 d=3 , the embedding (1.1) H 0 ​ ( curl , Ω ) ∩ H ⁡ ( div , Ω ) ↪ L 2 ​ ( Ω ) 3 H_{0}(\rot;\Omega)\cap H(\mathrm{div};\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^{2}(\Omega)^{3} is compact for a broad class of rather nonsmooth bounded domains Ω ⊆ ℝ 3 \Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{3} . Previously, Ω \Omega was required to be at least a C 1 , 1 C^{1,1} -domain in which case the continuous embedding H 0 ​ ( curl , Ω ) ∩ H ⁡ ( div , Ω ) ↪ H 1 ​ ( Ω ) 3 , H_{0}(\rot;\Omega)\cap H(\mathrm{div};\Omega)\hookrightarrow H^{1}(\Omega)^{3}, provided by a Gaffney-type estimate together with the classical Rellich–Kondrachov selection theorem, would yield the compactness statement for ( 1.1 ); see, e.g., [ 9 , Theorem 8.6] for a mere historical reference and a proof for C 5 C^{5} -domains. Weck [ 21 ] was the first to bypass Gaffney’s estimate and still recover compactness of ( 1.1 ) for certain singular domains with a bootstrapping argument in the dimension of the domain. Later, in [ 20 ] , Weber provided a perspective on the compactness of ( 1.1 ) with the main technical ingredient of Calderon’s extension theorem. We note in passing that this is also the circle of ideas in [ 2 ] , tied together with regular potentials. Here we shall revisit the seminal work [ 13 ] of Picard and the corresponding proof of the Maxwell compactness property. The key for [ 13 ] to work is two-fold: the tailored setting provided by differential forms and a Gaffney estimate for the cube. Even though the proof in [ 13 ] is very elegant and comparatively simple, the main ingredients might be rather inaccessible to many due to either the rather involved machinery of differential forms or the elusive Gaffney estimate. Even though well-known, the proof of the latter inequality appears to be technically demanding in many textbooks and articles, being based on an integration-by-parts formula involving the curvature of the boundary of the underlying domain; see, e.g., [ 1 , 4 , 7 , 12 , 14 ] . In any case some more theory needs to be appended, which is rooted in regularity theory for solutions of PDEs, or systems thereof, on smooth/convex domains; see, e.g., the proof in [ 10 ] or the rather recent work [ 11 ] . Thus, an independent proof without a rather strong background in both differential forms and regularity theory for PDEs appears to be missing in the literature. Hence, here we provide a proof of the compactness of ( 1.1 ) for weak Lipschitz domains without resorting to the Calderon extension theorem, regularity theory for PDE systems or a demanding integration by parts formula. In fact, by using functional analytic (‘soft’) arguments mainly, we reduce the amount of explicit computations to a minimum and, thus, only by using L 2 L^{2} -completeness of the Fourier basis functions, we shall establish Gaffney’s estimate on the cube and then close the elementary argument for the compactness statement via explicit transformation rules for the Euclidean case, not needing to resort to the calculus of differential forms. The argument being essentially the same for any dimension, we thus provide an independent proof of the following statement; for the explicit definition of ‘weak Lipschitz’, we refer to the main body of the present text. Theorem 1.1 (Picard–Weber–Weck selection theorem) . Let Ω ⊆ ℝ d \Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be a bounded, weak Lipschitz domain. Then, the embedding H 0 ​ ( Curl , Ω ) ∩ H ⁡ ( div , Ω ) ↪ L 2 ​ ( Ω ) d H_{0}(\Rot;\Omega)\cap H(\mathrm{div};\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^{2}(\Omega)^{d} is compact. Remark 1.2 . (a) The operator Curl \Rot is the (scaled) skew-symmetric part of the Jacobian and Curl ∘ \Rotcirc is the same with homogeneous boundary conditions; see Definition 2.2 . Similarly, div \mathrm{div} is the divergence operator with maximal L 2 L^{2} -domain and div ∘ \divcirc is the corresponding operator with homogeneous boundary conditions; see Definition 2.1 . We write H 0 ​ ( Curl , Ω ) := D ⁡ ( Curl ∘ Ω ) H_{0}(\Rot;\Omega):=D(\Rotcirc_{\Omega}) and H 0 ​ ( div , Ω ) := D ⁡ ( div ∘ Ω ) H_{0}(\mathrm{div};\Omega):=D(\divcirc_{\Omega}) . (b) The corresponding statement with the other boundary conditions, i.e., compactness of H ⁡ ( Curl , Ω ) ∩ H 0 ​ ( div , Ω ) ↪ L 2 ​ ( Ω ) d , H(\Rot;\Omega)\cap H_{0}(\mathrm{div};\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^{2}(\Omega)^{d}, is also true and follows by the same reasoning as the proof of Theorem 1.1 . We shall comment on the necessary adjustments for this case in the places, where they are necessary. A major application of Gaffney’s inequality is in the analysis of mixed finite element methods for Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman [ 5 , 6 , 8 , 17 ] and Fokker–Planck–Kolmogorov equations [ 18 , 16 ] . This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 , we go straight to proving the selection theorem. This will be subject to a Gaffney (in)equality for cubes and a transformation theorem, both of which are proven in the subsequent sections. For the former, some functional analytic results need to be established first; see Section 3 . In Section 4 , we present a self-contained proof of the Gaffney result for cubes. Finally, in Section 5 , we provide a proof of the transformation theorem, which concludes the article.

Email address: yishenglimysl@tamu.edu , Timo Sprekeler Timo Sprekeler Department of Mathematics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX 77843, USA. Email address: timo.sprekeler@tamu.edu and Marcus Waurick Marcus Waurick Institut für Angewandte Analysis, Technische Universität Bergakademie Freiberg, Germany. Email address: marcus.waurick@math.tu-freiberg.de Date: August 31, 2026 Abstract. Revisiting the rationale provided by Picard in the seminal paper [ 13 ] , we provide an independent, self-contained proof of the Maxwell compactness property for weak Lipschitz domains in the Euclidean setting, detouring technical complications like the differential forms setting, Gaffney’s inequality for smooth domains, Calderon’s extension theorem or regularity theory for PDEs, or systems thereof, on smooth domains that are used in this context. As a by-product we provide an independent proof of the classical Gaffney estimate for cubes using only L 2 L^{2} -completeness of the Fourier bases. Key words and phrases: Maxwell compactness property, Gaffney estimate, weak Lipschitz domains 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification 46E35, 47F05, 58J10 1. Introduction This paper is concerned with a by-now classical compactness result for differential forms going back to several articles by Weck [ 21 ] , Weber [ 20 ] , and Picard [ 13 ] . The main contribution of all of these results is that, for the sake of the argument expressed in dimension d = 3 d=3 , the embedding (1.1) H 0 ​ ( curl , Ω ) ∩ H ⁡ ( div , Ω ) ↪ L 2 ​ ( Ω ) 3 H_{0}(\rot;\Omega)\cap H(\mathrm{div};\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^{2}(\Omega)^{3} is compact for a broad class of rather nonsmooth bounded domains Ω ⊆ ℝ 3 \Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{3} . Previously, Ω \Omega was required to be at least a C 1 , 1 C^{1,1} -domain in which case the continuous embedding H 0 ​ ( curl , Ω ) ∩ H ⁡ ( div , Ω ) ↪ H 1 ​ ( Ω ) 3 , H_{0}(\rot;\Omega)\cap H(\mathrm{div};\Omega)\hookrightarrow H^{1}(\Omega)^{3}, provided by a Gaffney-type estimate together with the classical Rellich–Kondrachov selection theorem, would yield the compactness statement for ( 1.1 ); see, e.g., [ 9 , Theorem 8.6] for a mere historical reference and a proof for C 5 C^{5} -domains. Weck [ 21 ] was the first to bypass Gaffney’s estimate and still recover compactness of ( 1.1 ) for certain singular domains with a bootstrapping argument in the dimension of the domain. Later, in [ 20 ] , Weber provided a perspective on the compactness of ( 1.1 ) with the main technical ingredient of Calderon’s extension theorem. We note in passing that this is also the circle of ideas in [ 2 ] , tied together with regular potentials. Here we shall revisit the seminal work [ 13 ] of Picard and the corresponding proof of the Maxwell compactness property. The key for [ 13 ] to work is two-fold: the tailored setting provided by differential forms and a Gaffney estimate for the cube. Even though the proof in [ 13 ] is very elegant and comparatively simple, the main ingredients might be rather inaccessible to many due to either the rather involved machinery of differential forms or the elusive Gaffney estimate. Even though well-known, the proof of the latter inequality appears to be technically demanding in many textbooks and articles, being based on an integration-by-parts formula involving the curvature of the boundary of the underlying domain; see, e.g., [ 1 , 4 , 7 , 12 , 14 ] . In any case some more theory needs to be appended, which is rooted in regularity theory for solutions of PDEs, or systems thereof, on smooth/convex domains; see, e.g., the proof in [ 10 ] or the rather recent work [ 11 ] . Thus, an independent proof without a rather strong background in both differential forms and regularity theory for PDEs appears to be missing in the literature. Hence, here we provide a proof of the compactness of ( 1.1 ) for weak Lipschitz domains without resorting to the Calderon extension theorem, regularity theory for PDE systems or a demanding integration by parts formula. In fact, by using functional analytic (‘soft’) arguments mainly, we reduce the amount of explicit computations to a minimum and, thus, only by using L 2 L^{2} -completeness of the Fourier basis functions, we shall establish Gaffney’s estimate on the cube and then close the elementary argument for the compactness statement via explicit transformation rules for the Euclidean case, not needing to resort to the calculus of differential forms.
